problems.plain_summary: Buyers now ask AI tools instead of searching, and the AI names only a few brands in its answer. Marketers can't see those answers, can't measure them, and can't change them. Your brand either gets named, or it doesn't exist.

problems.definition: Ad platforms now expose a single AI-optimized objective (Performance Max, Advantage+, agentic buying assistants) while removing placement, query and creative-level reporting, leaving teams unable to determine what the platform actually caused or how to steer it.
problems.why_unsolved: Platform-reported conversions are modeled and self-attributed; the diagnostic data needed to audit them is deliberately withheld or aggregated. The accepted substitutes both fail at scale: geo/holdout experiments are underpowered for most budgets and channel mixes and take weeks per read, and open-source MMM (Meridian, Robyn) requires experiment calibration that the same teams cannot run, produces wide credible intervals, and yields different answers from different vendors on the same data with no accepted validation standard or benchmark. Platforms also change optimization behavior mid-flight, breaking the stationarity assumptions MMM depends on.

problems.canonical_name: Provable Downstream Consent, Deletion and Purpose Enforcement
problems.definition: Teams can capture consent and opt-out signals at the edge but cannot prove those signals are honored across the warehouse, activation tools, ad platform audiences, and models already trained on the data.
problems.why_unsolved: Consent is captured as an event, but the stack propagates copies: reverse ETL syncs, uploaded hashed-email audiences at Meta/Google, partner co-op data, agency-held segments, and ML features derived from the person. There is no standard machine-readable purpose/consent token that travels with a record through those hops, and no mechanism to remove an individual's contribution from an already-trained propensity or lookalike model short of retraining. Universal opt-out mechanisms (GPC) are now legally mandatory in several US states but are a browser-level signal with no defined mapping to server-side or CRM-held records. Auditing is manual, so most companies attest rather than verify.

problems.plain_summary: People opt out of tracking, and companies promise to honor it. But their data gets copied into many other systems, and no one can prove the opt-out followed it. One missed copy is a broken promise and a legal risk.

problems.canonical_name: Governance and Review of Generative Marketing Content at Volume
problems.definition: Generation capacity vastly exceeds a company's ability to verify that output is factually correct, claim-substantiated, rights-clear, on-brand, and properly disclosed, so throughput is capped by human review rather than by the model.
problems.why_unsolved: There is no reliable automated checker for the things review actually catches: substantiation of a performance claim against approved source material, regulated-industry constraints (MLR, FINRA), licensing scope of a stock or model-trained asset, and consistency with brand meaning rather than brand color values. Brand-governance tools verify surface attributes; they cannot adjudicate semantics or claims. Provenance standards (C2PA) are not carried through ad-serving and social pipelines, so labeling obligations cannot be discharged by metadata alone. EU AI Act transparency duties for synthetic content became applicable in August 2026 with no settled guidance on what constitutes adequate disclosure for marketing creative, which converts a quality problem into a compliance problem.

problems.plain: checking AI-written marketing before it ships
problems.plain_summary: AI can write endless marketing content, but someone still has to check every claim, right, and rule. Review is slow and human. So the bottleneck is no longer making content. It is proving the content is safe to ship.

problems.canonical_name: Governed Semantic Context Layer for Agents and Activation
problems.definition: AI agents can now call marketing systems, but nobody has a reliable way to give them correct, permissioned, semantically unambiguous context — so agent output is confidently wrong in ways that look plausible.
problems.why_unsolved: MCP standardized transport and tool discovery, not meaning or entitlements. There is still no shared semantic layer defining what 'active customer,' 'qualified lead' or 'revenue' means across CRM, CDP, warehouse and ad platforms, and no field-level permission or row-level security model that follows an agent across tools — so teams either over-scope agent access (leak and compliance risk) or under-scope it (useless agent). The spec surface is also still moving: the July 2026 stateless MCP revision invalidated architectures built a year earlier, so integration work does not compound.

problems.plain: agreeing on what basic terms like "customer" mean
problems.plain_summary: Every system defines basic words like 'customer' and 'revenue' a little differently. People paper over the gaps. AI agents don't. They act on the wrong meaning with full confidence.

problems.canonical_name: Safe, Auditable Agent Execution in Martech Systems
problems.definition: Teams want agents that actually act — change budgets, send campaigns, edit audiences, update CRM records — but current SaaS permissioning, audit, and rollback models were built for humans and cannot contain an autonomous actor.
problems.why_unsolved: Martech tools authenticate agents as a human seat or a broad OAuth scope, so there is no per-agent identity, least-privilege scope, or spend/blast-radius cap; audit logs record the borrowed human. MCP connectors proliferated faster than any authorization or provenance model, and prompt injection through the marketing data an agent reads (inbound emails, reviews, web pages, ticket text) remains unmitigated. Most systems of engagement have no transactional rollback for a sent send or a spent budget, so approval gates degrade to a human rubber-stamping every action, which erases the gain.

problems.plain: letting AI agents act without breaking things
problems.plain_summary: Marketers want AI agents that take real actions: move budgets, send campaigns, edit records. But today's tools can't give an agent its own identity, limits, or undo button. One bad action could hit thousands of customers.

problems.definition: When an AI agent browses, compares, and transacts on a user's behalf, marketers cannot tell agent from human, cannot apply consent or personalization correctly, cannot attribute the sale to a touchpoint, and cannot decide whether to serve, block, or price the request.
problems.why_unsolved: There is no widely honored signaling standard for 'this is an agent acting for an identified user with these permissions.' User-agent strings and IP ranges are unreliable and easily spoofed; bot-management systems classify agents as fraud, while agentic commerce protocols (ACP, AP2) standardize payment authorization but not marketing-relevant identity, consent state, or touchpoint provenance. Consent frameworks (TCF, US state opt-outs) assume a human viewing a banner. Analytics tools have no labeled ground-truth set for agent sessions, so even measuring the volume is guesswork, and ad verification cannot certify a human viewed an impression an agent fetched.

problems.plain: telling AI agents apart from real people
problems.plain_summary: More and more website visits come from AI agents acting for real people. Sites can't tell agent from human. So they can't decide whom to serve, whom to block, or who actually bought.

problems.definition: There is no dependable way to recognize, suppress, frequency-cap or personalize for the same consenting person across browsers, apps, CTV, commerce media, CRM and offline interactions. This creates both wasted reach and privacy risk.
problems.why_unsolved: No identifier is simultaneously ubiquitous, accurate, durable and acceptable under differing laws and platform policies. Deterministic IDs have limited coverage, probabilistic matching has uncertain error rates, and clean rooms can compare only the identities and data their participants already possess.

problems.plain: recognizing the same person across devices
problems.plain_summary: The same person shows up as different IDs across phones, browsers, TVs, and stores. There is no legal, reliable way to connect them. So brands repeat ads to people they already reached and miss the ones they wanted.

problems.definition: Marketing systems still cannot optimize a customer's overall experience across email, messaging, web, apps, advertising, commerce and service channels. Most optimize the next action inside one channel while creating contradictory offers, excessive contact or locally optimal but globally harmful outcomes.
problems.why_unsolved: Channel platforms expose uneven APIs and delayed feedback, customer state is incomplete, and there is no agreed objective function balancing conversion, margin, fatigue, service outcomes and long-term value. Organizational ownership and independent channel budgets further prevent a single decision layer from controlling execution.
aliases: Cross-channel journey orchestration with global control
Sub-Second Omnichannel State Orchestration
problems.plain_summary: Each channel optimizes its own messages. No system looks at the whole customer and coordinates. So one person gets clashing offers from the same brand in the same week.

pending_review.canonical_name: Machine-Readable Commerce Layer and Agent Protocol Interoperability
pending_review.definition: Brands have no canonical, real-time, structured representation of catalog, price, availability, delivery and policy that agents can consume — and no way to receive customer or performance data back when a transaction is agent-brokered.
pending_review.why_unsolved: Product truth is scattered across PIM, ERP, CMS and storefront with conflicting values, and the emerging protocol layer is fragmented across competing specs (ACP, UCP, AP2, card-network agent schemes) with no settled analytics or identity semantics, so merchants integrate multiple times and still receive thin, non-joinable order context. The commercial terms of the data exchange are also unsettled, as the crawler-payment fights show.
pending_review.reason: Supply-side readiness — canonical structured catalog/price/policy data and fragmented agent commerce protocols — is a distinct friction from identifying agent traffic or containing internal agents.

pending_review.canonical_name: Loss of B2B Account and Buying-Group Intent Signal
pending_review.definition: The breakdown of account-based intent tracking caused by remote-work network masking and non-trackable private community research channels.
pending_review.why_unsolved: Widespread hybrid work and VPN adoption render static IP-to-company mapping tables increasingly inaccurate, while key buyer research has shifted to dark social networks, private Slack groups, and internal AI query tools inaccessible to traditional intent vendors.
pending_review.reason: No existing entry covers account-based intent detection breaking down under VPN/remote work and dark-social research.
